# Chicago Facade Compliance: Keeping Condo Boards Project-Ready

CenterPoint Association Management Published September 5, 2026 3 min read

The practical answer for a Chicago condominium board: facade obligations are set by the Chicago Municipal Code and administered by the City's buildings department, and the requirements that apply to your building depend on its height, construction, and other characteristics. Your board should confirm its specific obligations, inspection cycle, and filing requirements directly with the City and with a licensed structural engineer or architect experienced in Chicago facade work, not from a neighbor's building, a vendor's sales pitch, or an article. Requirements and administrative procedures change, so verify current rules before each cycle.

What every board can act on regardless of building type is the planning discipline. Facade programs are multi-year, capital-intensive projects with engineering, permitting, contractor selection, resident disruption, and financing components. Boards that treat facade work as a scheduled capital program rather than an emergency avoid the worst outcomes: rushed contractor selection, emergency special assessments, and repeated scaffolding mobilizations.

## Start With Verified Facts About Your Building
Before budgeting anything, assemble the building's factual profile: height, number of stories, exterior wall assemblies, year built, and the history of prior facade inspections, reports, permits, and repairs. Many associations have this information scattered across former management companies. Reconstructing it is a worthwhile one-time project because engineers will ask for it, and lenders and buyers will too.

### Confirm Requirements With the City and Your Professional
Ask your engineer to state in writing which ordinance requirements apply to your building, what the inspection scope and reporting obligations are, and when the next filing is due. Ask the City directly if anything is unclear. Boards should never assume a requirement has been satisfied because a report exists somewhere in the files.

Facade programs are a core part of [high-rise condominium management](https://www.centerpointmgmt.com/services/high-rise-condominium-management) in Chicago.

## Choosing the Right Professionals
Facade work generally involves two distinct roles. A licensed **structural engineer or architect** performs the assessment, prepares repair documents, and administers construction. A **restoration contractor** performs the work. Keeping these roles separate protects the association: the professional who designs and inspects the repair should not be the party being paid to perform it. Ask for Chicago-specific facade experience, references from similar buildings, and current insurance certificates.

## Budgeting and Financing the Program
Facade repairs are typically among the largest single expenditures a vintage building will face. Boards generally consider some combination of reserve funds, a special assessment, and association financing. Each has consequences for owners and for resale, and the mechanics of adopting a special assessment are governed by the Illinois Condominium Property Act and your declaration. Ask association counsel to walk the board through notice, owner rights, and approval requirements before you commit publicly to a funding approach.

## Board Checklist for Facade Readiness

- Compile a complete facade file: prior reports, permits, repair invoices, warranties, and correspondence.
- Confirm in writing which City requirements apply to your building and when the next obligation is due.
- Require a written repair scope with priority tiers: life-safety, near-term, and deferrable.
- Build a multi-year capital plan that funds the program before it becomes urgent.
- Ask counsel to review the funding mechanism and any owner notice requirements.
- Competitively bid the construction work using the engineer's specifications, not contractor-authored scopes.
- Verify contractor licensing, insurance, and permits before mobilization.
- Publish a resident communication plan covering scaffolding, access, noise, and balcony restrictions.
- Retain the closeout package: final report, permits, photos, warranties, and payment records.

Also useful: [High-rise life-safety planning](https://www.centerpointmgmt.com/blog/chicago-condo-life-safety-board-planning).

## Where Management Adds Value
Facade programs succeed or fail on coordination. Consistent maintenance coordination, disciplined financial management, and organized board support keep engineering, permitting, bidding, and resident communication on one timeline. CenterPoint works with condominium boards throughout [Chicago](https://www.centerpointmgmt.com/property-management-chicago) on multi-year capital programs.

This article is educational information for association boards, not legal or engineering advice. Confirm current City of Chicago requirements with the department of buildings and retain a licensed design professional and association counsel for your building.
